newsitem.title: USA: Zedillo says party may lose 2000 election - paper.
newsitem.headline: Zedillo says party may lose 2000 election - paper.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo said in an interview published on Sunday that recent election results raised doubts that his ruling party would remain in power.

Speaking with the Chicago Tribune's correspondent in Mexico City, Zedillo conceded that the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) might well lose the presidency in 2000 after 70 years of uninterrupted rule.

"I can't tell you that automatically whoever is the PRI candidate is going to be the next president of Mexico, because now we have arrived at a true democratic system," Zedillo told the Tribune in a 90-minute interview conducted on Friday.

"And the other chaps," he said, referring to candidates from the two opposition parties that made great strides against the PRI in July 6 elections, "will be there to compete very intensely with a good probability to be successful."
Zedillo said the PRI had gotten a respectable 42 percent of the popular vote.
But he also spoke of an urgent need to implement a true "rule of law" in Mexico and expressed his desire to rid the country of official corruption.

"The party itself has never promoted, as an institution, corruption," he told the Tribune. "But what I told them," he said, referring to a speech to party leaders last week, "is that they have been lazy to denounce that."
"Corruption is not a phenomenom that can be dated back a few years. Unfortunately, our cultural traditions, certain practices, even from colonial times, have lent themselves to corruption," he said.
He praised the competing parties for their "terrific" marketing effort and acknowledged that reforms, though they could end up hurting the ruling party, were necessary.
Why? "Because we want democracy. Because we want all voices, all opinions of Mexican society reflected in the political spectrum," he was quoted as saying.
"I think it is now clear that we are moving quite convincingly into a three-party system. I don't know if (the PRI) will be first or second, but it will be a major player," he told the Tribune.

"The Mexican people will be watching closely whether (the other parties) use their new power, or whether they abuse their new power. Those parties, even if they didn't have the right democratic attitude, they will have the political instinct that they will be watched as much as the PRI," Zedillo said.
